paras: The Hartford City lynch mob was a manhunt and jail search in and near Hartford City, Indiana, on August 3, 1903, in which hundreds of men and boys hunted two unnamed Black men accused of mutilating George Hershey, a 19-year-old farm youth. The men were never found, and a crowd of about 500 at the county jail left peacefully after the sheriff let it search the building. Wire reports spread the story as a lynching in the making, while Indiana papers soon doubted the boy's account, which the Indianapolis Journal later called "altogether mythical."

Hershey said he was hunting squirrels on his father's farm southwest of Hartford City when two Black men seized him, searched him for money and cut him with a knife. The wire called him "an invalid" and his attackers "two prowling negroes."

His father, by the wire account, "called for volunteers to wreak vengeance on the fleeing negroes," and about 200 men and boys joined the chase. The Journal put the number at nearly 300 and had the sheriff leading them, while the wire said he and his deputies "followed the mob to prevent a lynching if possible." A Butte bulletin that day said the men were surrounded and "a mob is bent on lynching them," but the search ended at nightfall without a trace.

That evening a rumor spread that the men had been secretly jailed. About 9 p.m. a crowd of "fully 500" gathered at the jail, and a committee demanded the keys from Sheriff Morrical. He opened the jail, and once assured the men were not there the crowd dispersed without violence; the correspondent thought a refusal would have led it to storm the jail. Armed men guarded the woods overnight, and residents then raised a $300 reward, while officers said captured men would not be brought to Hartford City.

The Journal expected the leaders of the jail crowd to be prosecuted. By August 20 Governor Durbin had asked the Blackford county judge and prosecutor what steps they had taken against the mob and had received no reply. On October 26 Judge Edwin C. Vaughn told the grand jury to investigate "the members of the mob who demanded the life of the negro assaulters of George Hershey." No report of indictments, a trial, or an arrest of the accused men appears in the coverage.

Outside Indiana the episode ran as one wire dispatch, printed on August 4 in the New-York Tribune, Wilmington Evening Journal and Wichita Daily Eagle and reprinted in weeklies as far as Nebraska through August 13. Most headlines treated the accusation as fact, such as "Negroes' Horrible Work on Boy" and "Fiendish Negroes Torture Invalid." Others headlined the mob: "Hoosiers Bent on Lynching" in the New York Herald and "Mob After Human Blood" in Butte. Short notices called Hershey "a white boy" or "a white cripple," and a Wisconsin digest said the jail "was stormed by a mob of 500 men," which the Indiana reports do not support.

The Indianapolis Journal, with a correspondent on the scene, followed the case longest and changed its framing. Its first report called the assailants "the fiends" and predicted that "Judge Lynch will preside at their funeral," yet noted that only the boy had seen them. By August 20 it wrote that the truth had emerged "too late to have prevented a probable lynching of any negroes who might have been so unfortunate as to have been in the mob's way." Neither the doubts nor the governor's inquiry appear in the out-of-state coverage found, and no Black newspaper's account was located.

The first night the Journal reported a rumor that the boy had injured himself, which he denied. An August 5 dispatch said "the impression prevails that there were no negroes," citing his untouched loaded shotgun and the twine and knife being his own, though his physician said the wounds could not be self-inflicted. An August 8 dispatch said his story was "now generally credited" because responsible persons had seen two Black men nearby. On August 20 the Journal stated, without naming a source, that the assault was "altogether mythical" and self-inflicted; no inquest or court finding appears in the coverage.

bases: Crowds of 200 to 500 hunted two Black men accused of mutilating a white youth and searched the county jail for them, with papers saying the mob was 'bent on lynching them'; no one was found or harmed (A1, A2, A3).
A crowd of hundreds acting without legal authority sought to lynch two Black men on an accusation of assault, but no one was caught or killed (A2, A3, A19); this was a threatened lynching only.

The manhunt and the threat of lynching are reported in the Indiana correspondent's account and the independent wire dispatch (A2, A3), and the jail search by the Journal and a Wisconsin digest (A2, A23); whether the underlying assault happened is contested (A17, A25, A26).

accounts.label: The boy's account (Indiana correspondent)
accounts.gist: Two Black men gagged him with plantain leaves, searched his pockets, took his penknife and mutilated him, one saying 'Kill him' and the other proposing to 'unman him' instead.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Two 'prowling negroes' seized an invalid boy at noon, searched him for money, stripped him and mutilated him with a knife; 200 men and boys gave chase and the sheriff followed to prevent a lynching.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal on the jail
accounts.gist: A crowd of 500 sent a committee to demand the keys on a rumor the men were inside; the sheriff let them search and they dispersed peacefully.

accounts.label: Doubters (Aug. 5 dispatch)
accounts.gist: Many, including some officers, believed there were no Black assailants: no one else saw them, the boy's loaded shotgun lay untouched, and the twine and knife were his own.

accounts.label: Aug. 8 dispatch
accounts.gist: The boy's story was again generally credited because responsible persons had seen two Black men in the vicinity.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal, Aug. 20
accounts.gist: Unattributed statement that the assault was 'altogether mythical' and self-inflicted, discovered too late to have prevented a probable lynching.

framing.detail: The wire story ran under headlines such as 'Negroes' Horrible Work on Boy', 'Fiendish Negroes Torture Invalid' and 'Negroes Maim Boy', presenting the boy's accusation as fact.

The Indianapolis Journal first called the accused 'the fiends' and predicted 'Judge Lynch will preside at their funeral', but reported doubts the same night and on Aug. 20 called the assault 'altogether mythical'.
The New York Herald ('Hoosiers Bent on Lynching') and Butte Inter Mountain ('Mob After Human Blood') headlined the mob rather than the crime.
The Plymouth Tribune printed the doubts ('His Story Is Doubted') and then a correction in the boy's favor ('Justice to George Hrshey').

info: Monday, August 3, 1903: alleged assault in the morning or at noon, manhunt that afternoon, crowd at the jail about 9 p.m.
Woods on the Hershey farm about three and a half miles southwest of Hartford City (the Willman woods), and the Hartford City jail
No one was harmed by the mob. Its targets were two unnamed Black men ('two negroes') whom George Hershey (also printed Hearshy, Hearshey, Nershey, Hearsney), 19, said had attacked him.
Accused by George Hershey of seizing him, searching him for money, and mutilating him with a knife while he hunted squirrels on his father's farm
Volunteers raised by the boy's father ('men and boys'), farmers, and a crowd at the jail that sent a committee to demand the keys; none named
The accused men were never found; the crowd dispersed from the jail without violence; the boy's account was doubted, then credited, then called 'altogether mythical'
